This is real, well-scoped engineering work once a specific stuck test is identified from a goroutine dump (item L229) — but as of this scope's investigation no such dump exists yet in the repo (no docs/ file or issue referencing a captured goroutine dump was found), so the concrete file:line target cannot be named until L229's capture happens; the SEARCH PATTERN itself, however, is fully specifiable now.

verified_anchors.expect: 0 hits, or only this TODO's own text — confirming the dump has not yet been captured/committed anywhere

why_tier: Once a specific goroutine dump names the stuck test, tracing an unbounded wait to its root cause needs real debugging judgment (is it a genuine deadlock, a slow real I/O call, or a test fixture issue), not mechanical grepping — but the SEARCH itself (candidate unbounded waits) can be pre-scoped now to speed up whoever does the diagnosis.
goal: Once item L229 produces a real goroutine dump naming the stuck test, use it to find the specific unbounded wait (WaitGroup.Wait, unbuffered/blocking channel receive, or mutex Lock() with no surrounding context/timeout) inside internal/database's test helpers that causes the ~200-280s -short-run stall, and fix it (bound the wait with a context deadline or timeout).
background: As a pre-scoping aid (not a substitute for the real dump): `grep -rn '\.Wait()\|<-.*chan\|\.Lock()' internal/database/*_test.go internal/database/dbtest/*.go` will enumerate CANDIDATE unbounded waits in the target package ahead of time, but the actual root cause must be confirmed against the real goroutine dump's stack trace, not guessed from this list alone — grepping for the pattern finds many benign waits and this repo's own memory explicitly warns against trusting a naming/pattern grep as a census of the real problem.
steps: 1. Wait for / obtain the goroutine dump captured per item L229's instruction from the next occurrence of the stuck-test CI failure (or from the ORIGINAL occurrence's Actions log if it is still retrievable via `gh run view --log` before its retention window expires).
2. From the dump, identify the specific goroutine(s) blocked and their stack trace, which names the exact file:line of the unbounded wait.

3. Fix that specific wait with a context deadline (t.Context() with timeout, or context.WithTimeout wrapping the blocking call) so it fails fast and names itself rather than consuming the whole package's test budget.
tests: A regression test asserting the specific fixed wait now has a bounded timeout — exact test name depends on which helper is found in step 2, cannot be named yet.
acceptance: The previously-stuck test now fails fast (seconds, not 200-280s) with a clear timeout error naming itself when the underlying condition it was waiting on is not met, verified with `go test ./internal/database/... -short -timeout 60s -v` showing no 200s+ single-test stalls.
edge_cases: The unbounded wait may be intentional in production code paths (only the TEST's use of it is unbounded) — fix only the test-side invocation with a timeout, do not weaken a production synchronization primitive to add one.
notes: Blocked on L229's artifact existing — cannot be executed with full precision today. The pre-scoping grep above is a starting point for whoever picks this up next, not a substitute for the real diagnosis.

title: Add a per-test deadline (t.Context()/context.WithTimeout) so a hang fails fast and names itself
verdict_evidence: NEEDS SCOPING: scout returned no exact_files — cannot enter the collision matrix. This is a general test-infrastructure improvement independent of finding the SPECIFIC L232 root cause — Go 1.24+ (this repo's go.mod, per CLAUDE.md, targets 1.24.0/1.25/1.26 features) supports `t.Context()` which is automatically cancelled on test timeout; adding this pattern to internal/database's slower/blocking-prone test helpers is actionable today without waiting on a goroutine dump.

verified_anchors.claim: the repo's Go version supports t.Context() (Go 1.24+)

why_tier: Requires judgment about WHICH tests/helpers in internal/database are the blocking-prone ones worth instrumenting (not a blind sweep across the whole package, which could mask genuine slow-but-legitimate tests with a too-tight timeout) — needs a look at the package's test helper structure first.
goal: Add per-test or per-helper timeouts (via t.Context() passed into blocking calls, or context.WithTimeout wrapping WaitGroup/channel waits) to internal/database's test helpers so an unbounded wait fails in seconds naming the specific test, rather than consuming the whole package's -short budget and reporting only the package name on timeout.
background: This is explicitly framed in the TODO as independent, lower-effort mitigation ('Consider...') distinct from L232's root-cause fix — it makes the NEXT occurrence of ANY unbounded wait (not just the one L232 targets) fail fast and self-diagnosing, which is valuable even before L232's specific root cause is found.
steps: 1. Identify internal/database's shared test-setup/teardown helpers (likely in internal/database/dbtest/ per earlier findings in this scope) that perform waits, locks, or spin up background goroutines per test.

2. Wrap the riskiest ones (WaitGroup.Wait, channel receive, Lock() calls found via the L232 pre-scoping grep) with `ctx := t.Context()` (auto-cancelled at the test's own timeout) or an explicit `context.WithTimeout(t.Context(), <bound>)` shorter than the package's overall -short budget, so an individual test's hang surfaces with THAT test's name rather than blowing the whole package's time allotment.

3. Pick a bound generously above legitimate slow-path duration (avoid flaking genuinely-slow-but-correct tests) — if unsure of a safe value, start with something like 30s per blocking call and adjust based on CI history.
tests: A synthetic test proving the pattern works: TestHelperX_TimesOutRatherThanHangs — deliberately trigger the never-satisfied wait condition in a controlled way (e.g. a channel that is never written to) and assert the test fails within the bound, not after the full package timeout.
acceptance: `go test ./internal/database/... -short -v` — a deliberately-broken wait (temporarily reintroduced for verification, then reverted) fails within the new bound rather than stalling the whole package.
edge_cases: Overly tight timeouts on legitimately slow (but correct) integration-style tests in internal/database could introduce NEW flakiness — pick bounds conservatively and validate against real CI run durations before tightening further.
anti_over_suppression: The bound must be generous enough that a genuinely slow-but-passing test does not start failing under normal CI load — validate against actual historical run times (see L238's cost-reduction angle) before picking a number, and treat any newly-introduced timeout-flake as a signal the bound was set too tight, not that the test itself is broken.
notes: Independent of L232/L238 — can be done in parallel/first, since it improves diagnosability for ANY future stall, not just the specific one still awaiting its goroutine dump.

title: Reduce internal/database's -short test-run wall-clock cost (currently 200-280s, most of the coverage gate's budget)
verdict_evidence: NEEDS SCOPING: scout returned no exact_files — cannot enter the collision matrix. This is a general test-performance item ('Reduce the wait-bound cost while there') distinct from the stuck-test investigation (L229/L232) — it targets the NORMAL (non-hung) run duration of internal/database's -short suite, which the TODO states is 200-280s and 'most of the coverage gate's budget on its own', independently actionable via standard Go test-perf techniques (parallelization, reducing redundant setup, profiling for the actual hot path) without needing the goroutine dump L232 depends on.

reuse.name: existing coverage-gate Makefile target this run time counts against

why_tier: Requires profiling (go test -short -v with timing, or `go test -short -json` timing analysis) to find the actual hot spots before optimizing — not a blind rewrite; genuine performance-analysis judgment.
goal: Profile internal/database's -short test suite to find what actually consumes the bulk of its 200-280s wall-clock time (shared expensive setup run per-test instead of per-package, serialized tests that could run with t.Parallel(), or genuinely slow I/O in a helper), and cut it meaningfully, since this consumes most of the make ci coverage gate's overall time budget.
background: Cutting this cost benefits every future CI run, not just the specific stuck-test scenario — worth doing independently of whether L232's root cause is ever found, since a 200-280s single-package run is expensive regardless of whether it occasionally also hangs.
steps: 1. Run `go test ./internal/database/... -short -v -json > /tmp/db_test_timing.json` and parse per-test durations (e.g. with `go tool test2json` output or a small script) to rank the slowest individual tests.

2. For the top offenders, check whether they share expensive per-test setup (e.g. a full Pebble DB open/close per test instead of a shared fixture with per-test namespacing) that could be hoisted to TestMain or a shared package-level fixture.

3. Check whether independent tests are unnecessarily serialized (missing `t.Parallel()`) where parallelization would be safe (no shared mutable global state) — internal/database tests using a real Pebble store per test are prime candidates if they don't already share one DB instance across parallel subtests with distinct key prefixes.
4. Apply the highest-leverage fix(es) found and re-measure.
tests: No new test needed — success is measured by the suite's own wall-clock time, not new assertions; ensure no existing test's correctness assumptions are broken by any added parallelism (check for shared mutable package-level state introduced by t.Parallel()).
acceptance: `time go test ./internal/database/... -short` shows a measurably lower wall-clock time than the 200-280s baseline, with the specific before/after numbers recorded in the PR description.
edge_cases: Adding t.Parallel() to tests that share an underlying Pebble DB instance without proper key-space isolation could introduce flaky cross-test interference — verify isolation before parallelizing, don't just add t.Parallel() everywhere.
notes: Independent of L229/L232 — this is pure performance work on the (usually) non-hung path.

title: Investigate why React silently drops a setState issued from setTimeout on a mounted class component inside a portal
verdict_evidence: NEEDS SCOPING: scout returned no exact_files — cannot enter the collision matrix. This is framed as an open research question with several hypotheses already ruled out by the item text (duplicate React copies, StrictMode, flushSync/startTransition/unstable_batchedUpdates, uncaught exceptions, unmounting) and one untested leading hypothesis (production-build React 18 concurrent-root update issued mid-render). Confirmed the mitigation currently shipped is narrower than the root cause: web/src/theme.ts's MuiMenu override still uses `transitionDuration: { enter: 225, exit: 0 }` (same pattern that failed 10/10 for Drawer on MUI v6 before `slotProps.transition.exit: false` was needed there), so any component still using the exit:0 pattern remains exposed to the same undiagnosed mechanism.

why_tier: Deep React-internals root-cause investigation with several hypotheses already exhausted and no clear next experiment specified — needs strong reasoning to design a new repro/instrumentation approach, not mechanical execution.
goal: Determine the actual mechanism by which a setState from a setTimeout inside a mounted class component inside a portal gets silently dropped in a production build, so that every component still relying on the narrower exit:0 mitigation (currently just MuiMenu, per theme.ts) can be evaluated for the same risk that hit Drawer, rather than waiting for each one to fail 10/10 independently.
background: Already ruled out per the item: duplicate React copies (single react@18.3.1, deduped), StrictMode (dev-only), flushSync/startTransition/unstable_batchedUpdates (absent from web/src), uncaught exceptions (none observed), unmounting (componentWillUnmount never runs, isMounted stays true).

Leading untested hypothesis: a production-build React 18 concurrent-root update issued while the root is mid-render, for which the dev-only warning that would normally name this problem does not fire in production.

The Drawer incident (2026-08-10) was fixed with `slotProps.transition.exit: false`, not `exit: 0` — exit:0 measured 20/20 pass on Drawer before later failing 10/10 on MUI v6, meaning exit:0 is not a reliable fix, just a probability-narrower. MuiMenu currently rides exit:0 only.
steps: 1. Reproduce a minimal case: a class component rendered via a portal (React Portal / MUI Modal root) with a setTimeout-issued setState, running against the PRODUCTION build (not vite dev server) — since StrictMode/dev warnings are explicitly ruled out as not applicable, the repro must use `npm run build` output, not `npm run dev`.

2. Instrument with React DevTools Profiler (or manual console logging around the class component's setState call and render/commit lifecycle) to determine: does the setState call itself fire (confirm the timer callback executes), does React schedule an update (check via a wrapping requestIdleCallback/scheduler hook if accessible), and does a render/commit actually occur for that fiber.

3. Specifically test the leading hypothesis: force the timing so the setTimeout fires while the concurrent root is mid-render of an unrelated update (e.g. trigger a large list re-render concurrently), and see if the drop reproduces reliably under that specific condition versus not reproducing when isolated.

4. If reproduced, minimize to the smallest possible repro component and either (a) file/document it as a known React concurrent-mode interaction with a workaround, or (b) identify a code-level fix specific to this codebase's usage pattern.

5. Regardless of root-cause outcome, audit web/src/theme.ts for every component still using `exit: 0` (currently MuiMenu only, confirmed) and evaluate whether it needs the same `slotProps.transition.exit: false` treatment that fixed Drawer, since exit:0 is now known to be an incomplete mitigation rather than a fix.
tests: A regression e2e or unit test that reproduces the drop reliably (if step 1-3 succeed) — without a reliable repro, this cannot be regression-tested, and the deliverable becomes a documented finding + a decision on whether to preemptively harden MuiMenu.
acceptance: A documented root-cause finding (even if the ultimate answer is 'confirmed unreproducible after N attempts under conditions X, Y, Z') exists, plus an explicit decision on whether MuiMenu's exit:0 needs upgrading to the exit:false pattern.
edge_cases: If the mechanism turns out to be React-version-specific (fixed in a later React 18.x patch or React 19), the fix may be an upgrade rather than a code workaround — check the currently pinned React version and its changelog for concurrent-root setState-drop fixes before assuming a local code fix is needed.
anti_over_suppression: N/A — this is root-cause research, not a filter/guard.
gate: npm --prefix web run lint && npm --prefix web test
notes: High uncertainty of convergence — flag to the coordinator as an investigation spike with a capped time budget rather than a guaranteed-deliverable ticket. The MuiMenu exit:0 audit in step 5 is the concrete, low-risk fallback deliverable even if the root-cause investigation does not converge.

Frontend: preview control renders in the chooser and triggers a request scoped to part 1's file ID.
acceptance: Manual: on a 40-part book in the chooser, click preview and confirm audio plays from the START of part 1, not from whichever file the row happens to reference, and that a large/malicious Range request cannot pull more than the capped duration server-side.
edge_cases: A book with zero files or a corrupted/unreadable part-1 file should show a clear 'preview unavailable' state, not a silent failure or a crash.

notes: The unbounded-read-caused-OOM caution is load-bearing — the server-side cap must be enforced independent of client-supplied Range headers, not merely a client-side convention that a malicious or buggy request could bypass.

Other candidate CreateBook call sites in files touching per-chapter/split logic (not yet checked in depth): internal/plugins/dedup/split_book_scan.go, internal/plugins/maintenance/fs_regroup_xml.go (only calls CreateBookFile, not CreateBook — ruled out), internal/itunes/service/fs_regroup_shape.go (0 SeriesID/CreateBook hits — ruled out), internal/scanner/scanner.go:2864 (`dst.SeriesID = scanned.SeriesID` — this assigns FROM an already-resolved scanned.SeriesID onto an existing dst row during a re-scan merge, not book creation from a copied ID; worth checking whether 'scanned' can itself carry a stale-but-plausible SeriesID under some merge-during-warmup race, but not yet confirmed).
steps: grep -rn "CreateBook(" internal/scanner internal/dedup internal/plugins internal/itunes --include=*.go | grep -v _test.go to get the full candidate list beyond the 3 already ruled out.

For each remaining candidate, check whether the &database.Book{...} literal or a subsequently-set field copies SeriesID from an existing/sibling Book struct rather than leaving it nil or calling resolveSeriesID.

Cross-reference book 01KZSX7TW6BZXJX11F8K6Y0DSZ and its 2026-08-11 22:36 siblings against the operations list for that exact minute (the TODO already ruled out 41 named ops for the whole day/next day — narrow to the single minute) to see if ANY op (even one not on the ruled-out list, e.g. a scan itself, which the TODO notes was suspiciously ABSENT from the operations list that day) was running.

Once the actual copy site is found, fix it to either call resolveSeriesID fresh for the new row or explicitly drop SeriesID when the source reference is unverified, per the standing rule 'never mint or propagate a dangling reference'.
tests: Once the source is found: a regression test in that package asserting a newly-created book never carries a SeriesID that doesn't resolve to an existing series row.
acceptance: The 6,893-count phantom-series-reference query (however it's currently run — check internal/database or a maintenance report op for it) shows 0 NEW phantom IDs appearing after the fix, re-verified against a fresh scan/regroup run in a sandbox.
edge_cases: A book intentionally created with SeriesID=nil (no series) must not be mistaken for the bug — only a non-nil SeriesID pointing at a NONEXISTENT series row is the defect.
